documents.title: Emergency: abdominal pain
documents.text: 17-year-old with severe cramping abdominal pain and vomiting. CT shows bowel wall thickening and free fluid. Resolved over two days without treatment. No diagnosis made.

documents.title: Surgery: suspected appendicitis
documents.text: Severe abdominal pain. Appendectomy performed. Pathology: normal appendix.

documents.title: Emergency: hand swelling
documents.text: Swelling of the right hand after carrying groceries. No hives or itching. Treated with antihistamine and steroids without clear benefit. Resolved in three days.

documents.title: Gastroenterology: recurrent attacks
documents.text: Recurrent attacks of abdominal pain every few months, each lasting two to three days. Endoscopy and colonoscopy normal. Impression: functional abdominal pain.

documents.title: Allergy: swelling episodes
documents.text: Episodes of facial and limb swelling without hives. Not on ACE inhibitor. C4 measured between attacks within reference range; hereditary angioedema considered less likely. Advised to carry antihistamines.

documents.title: Emergency: facial swelling
documents.text: Lip and tongue swelling with hoarse voice. No hives. Epinephrine, antihistamine, and steroids given with slow improvement over 24 hours. Observed overnight.

documents.title: Primary care: attack frequency
documents.text: Swelling and abdominal attacks more frequent since starting oral contraceptive. Family history: mother had episodes of throat swelling, never diagnosed.

documents.title: Emergency: abdominal attack
documents.text: Severe abdominal pain with ascites on ultrasound. Resolved in 48 hours. Discharged with diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain.

documents.title: Primary care: review
documents.text: Patient asks why antihistamines never help. No C1 inhibitor level or function test is documented in the record.
